title: Crash and hang analysis: BSODs, dumps & WinDbg basics
summary: Turn a blue screen or a frozen application into a named root cause by reading crash dumps in WinDbg. Configure dump capture, resolve symbols, and run the analysis commands that point at the faulting module.
objectives: Configure Windows to capture the right dump type for kernel and user crashes
Resolve symbols correctly so WinDbg can name modules and functions
Run !analyze -v and interpret the bugcheck code and faulting module
Distinguish a hang from a crash and capture a manual dump of a frozen process
Read a basic call stack to attribute a fault to a specific driver or DLL
Decide when a crash is a driver defect versus corrupted state versus hardware

quiz.q: A machine bugchecks intermittently and you need stack and driver detail but disk space is limited. Which dump type is the best default for kernel crashes?
options: Active memory dump of user pages only
No dump — rely on the event log
quiz.why: A kernel memory dump captures kernel-mode memory — enough to name the faulting driver and read the stack — without the size of a complete dump. Automatic dump is the modern default and sizes the page file accordingly.

quiz.q: WinDbg shows '*** ERROR: Module load completed but symbols could not be loaded'. What is the correct fix?
options: Set the symbol path to the Microsoft symbol server and reload
quiz.why: Without symbols WinDbg cannot map addresses to function names. Setting .sympath to the public symbol server (srv*) and running .reload resolves the stack to readable names.

quiz.q: !analyze -v reports a bugcheck and names a third-party driver in MODULE_NAME and IMAGE_NAME. What is the most defensible next conclusion?
options: That driver is the prime suspect for the proximate cause; verify its version and known issues
quiz.why: MODULE_NAME/IMAGE_NAME point to the code executing at the fault. It is the prime proximate suspect — but a Tier 3 engineer still verifies version, signing, and known issues before declaring root cause, since a driver can fault on corrupted state it did not create.

quiz.q: An application is frozen but not crashed. How do you get a dump for analysis?
options: Wait for it to crash on its own
Capture a user-mode dump of the live process with ProcDump or Task Manager 'Create dump file'
quiz.why: A hang produces no crash dump on its own. You capture the live process state — ProcDump (e.g. procdump -ma) or Task Manager's Create dump file — then analyse the threads and locks to see what it is waiting on.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does the bugcheck code (e.g. 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL) tell you?
quiz.answer: It classifies the kind of illegal operation the kernel detected (here, a driver accessed pageable memory at too high an IRQL), which narrows the failure mode and often points directly at a driver category before you even read the stack.
quiz.why: The bugcheck code is the kernel's classification of what rule was violated, giving you a head start on the failure mode and likely culprit class.

quiz.q: Why might a crash that names a Microsoft driver still NOT be a Microsoft bug?
quiz.answer: A faulting Microsoft driver may simply be the code that finally tripped over memory already corrupted by a different third-party driver upstream; the visible faulting module is the victim, so you read the full stack and check for other recently loaded or unsigned drivers before assigning blame.
quiz.why: The faulting frame is where the crash surfaced, not necessarily where the corruption originated, so attribution requires reading the stack and surrounding context, not just MODULE_NAME.

body_markdown:
## A crash is data, not a mystery

A blue screen — a **bugcheck** — is the kernel deliberately stopping because continuing would corrupt the system. That stop produces a **crash dump**: a snapshot of memory you can read after the fact. A frozen app produces no dump on its own, but you can force one. Either way, the crash is not a mystery; it is evidence waiting for a debugger.

## Capture the right dump

Before you can analyse, you must capture. For kernel crashes the **Kernel memory dump** (or the modern **Automatic** setting) is the right default: it holds enough kernel memory to name the faulting driver and read the stack, without the disk cost of a **Complete** dump.

```powershell
# Confirm the configured dump type (CrashDumpEnabled: 1=Complete,2=Kernel,7=Automatic)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl' |
  Select-Object CrashDumpEnabled, DumpFile, AutoReboot
```

Kernel dumps land at `%SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP`. Minidumps go to `%SystemRoot%\Minidump`.

## Symbols first, always

WinDbg maps raw addresses to function names using **symbols**. Without them every frame is a hex address and the analysis is useless. Point WinDbg at the Microsoft public symbol server before anything else.

```text
.sympath srv*C:\symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols
.reload /f
```

If you ever see *"symbols could not be loaded"*, fix the symbol path and `.reload` — do not interpret a stack until names resolve.

## !analyze -v: the first real command

The workhorse is `!analyze -v` ("analyze, dash v" for verbose). It decodes the **bugcheck code**, identifies the likely **faulting module**, and prints the stack at the point of failure.

```text
!analyze -v

*** look for these lines ***
BUGCHECK_CODE:  D1            (DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL)
MODULE_NAME:    somedriver
IMAGE_NAME:     somedriver.sys
FAILURE_BUCKET_ID: ...
```

The bugcheck code classifies *what rule was broken*. `MODULE_NAME`/`IMAGE_NAME` name the code executing at the fault — your prime proximate suspect. But stay disciplined: a faulting module can be the *victim* of corruption another driver caused upstream. Read the full stack with `k`, and check for recently loaded or unsigned drivers with `lm` before assigning root cause.

## Hangs: capture the frozen state

A hang never bugchecks, so you capture the live process. Use **ProcDump** or Task Manager's *Create dump file*.

```text
procdump -ma <pid-or-name> C:\evidence\hang.dmp
```

Open the user-mode dump, run `!analyze -v -hang`, and inspect threads with `~*k` to see what each is waiting on — a lock, a remote call, or a deadlock between two threads. Look for a thread blocked inside a critical section while another thread owns it: that ownership cycle is the signature of a classic deadlock, and the call stacks usually name the component responsible.

## Your task

On a test VM, confirm the configured dump type via the `CrashControl` registry key and set it to Automatic if it is not. Trigger or obtain a kernel dump (a test crash, or an existing MEMORY.DMP), open it in WinDbg, set the symbol path to the public server, and run `!analyze -v`. Record the bugcheck code, the named module, and the top of the stack from `k`. Then capture a user-mode dump of a deliberately hung process with ProcDump, run `~*k`, and write one sentence on what the main thread was waiting on. Conclude with whether your evidence points to a driver defect, corrupted state, or hardware.

slides.narration: The workhorse command is bang analyze dash v — analyze, verbose. It decodes the bugcheck code, identifies the likely faulting module, and prints the stack at the point of failure. The bugcheck code classifies what rule was broken — for example, D one means a driver touched pageable memory at too high an I R Q L. Module name and image name point at the code that was executing when it faulted. That's your prime proximate suspect.

slides.title: The faulting module may be the victim
bullets: MODULE_NAME is where the crash surfaced, not always its origin.
A driver can fault on corruption another driver caused.
Read the full stack with k.
Check recently loaded or unsigned drivers with lm.
slides.narration: Now stay disciplined. The faulting module is where the crash surfaced — not necessarily where the corruption began. A Microsoft driver can fault simply because it tripped over memory that a third-party driver corrupted upstream. So before you blame the named module, read the full stack with the k command, and list the loaded modules with l m to spot anything recently loaded or unsigned. The visible faulting frame might be the victim, not the culprit.

slides.title: Hangs: capture the frozen state
bullets: A hang never bugchecks — no automatic dump.
Capture the live process with ProcDump or Task Manager.
Open the user-mode dump and inspect every thread.
Look for a lock, a remote call, or a deadlock.
slides.narration: A hang never bugchecks, so there's no automatic dump. You capture the live process yourself, with ProcDump — proc-dump dash m a — or Task Manager's Create dump file. Open that user-mode dump and run tilde star k to walk every thread's stack. You're looking for what each thread is waiting on: a lock, a slow remote call, or two threads deadlocked against each other. The wait, not the work, is the story in a hang.

slides.title: Driver, state, or hardware?
bullets: Repeated same bugcheck + same module: driver defect.
Random codes, varying modules: corrupted state or hardware.
Verify driver version, signing, and known issues.
Let the pattern across crashes guide attribution.
slides.narration: Finally, classify the root cause. If you see the same bugcheck code naming the same module across repeated crashes, that's a strong driver-defect signal — verify its version, signing, and known issues. If you see random bugcheck codes naming different modules each time, suspect corrupted state or failing hardware, like bad memory. Let the pattern across multiple crashes guide attribution; a single dump rarely settles it on its own.
